articles.title: Nepal-Tibet border flood: what is known and what remains uncertain
articles.subtitle: Later official figures sharply raised the toll after the Bhote Koshi disaster, while access and communications complicated the count
articles.excerpt: A source-based update on the Bhote Koshi flood, the changing casualty estimates and the recovery questions facing remote Himalayan communities.
articles.author: elena-marsh

content.text: A destructive flood moved through the Bhote Koshi border corridor on August 26 after a high-mountain slope failure and temporary river blockage. The surge damaged transport links, settlements and energy infrastructure in difficult terrain. Early official counts were incomplete because roads and communications were cut.
How the event unfolded

Reports from the first days described a mass of ice and rock entering a tributary above the border corridor, temporarily holding back water before a surge traveled downstream. Precise attribution in a remote high-altitude catchment takes time: satellite analysis, field access and hydrological records all contribute, and early explanations should not be treated as a final scientific assessment.
Why the numbers changed

On August 27, authorities were reporting at least 390 deaths and about 1,400 people missing across affected areas. By September 7, Nepal's disaster management agency said more than 1,300 people had died and roughly 5,000 were missing, according to the Associated Press. The later figures supersede the headline counts in the first version of this post.

A missing-person total is not the same as a confirmed death toll. Displaced residents, damaged phone networks and incomplete local registers can all enlarge the number of people who are temporarily unaccounted for. The figures should therefore be read with their dates and sources attached.
The longer recovery

Immediate work centered on rescue, shelter, medical care and restoring access. Recovery also raises longer questions about bridge design, warning systems and development in narrow valleys exposed to landslides and glacial hazards. Nepal's government issued an international relief appeal, while health authorities published response updates for affected districts.

This post was updated on September 9 to replace early casualty estimates with later figures and to make the uncertainty around missing-person counts explicit. The linked official notices and subsequent assessments should be consulted for further changes.

articles.title: Iran and Oman propose temporary shipping corridor through Strait of Hormuz
articles.subtitle: The plan aims to restore navigation through mine clearance and phased traffic rules
articles.excerpt: Iran and Oman have outlined a phased framework for a temporary joint shipping corridor and a mine-clearing mission through the Strait of Hormuz, even as President Trump says the U.S. Navy has already cleared the waterway's main channel and traffic has surged as Tehran's grip on the strait weakens.
articles.author: elena-marsh

toc.text: Iran's weakening grip on the strait

content.text: Iran and Oman have outlined a phased framework for a temporary, jointly managed shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, along with a mission to clear mines from the waterway, marking one of the clearest steps yet toward restoring full commercial navigation through the critical passage after months of disruption.
What the proposal includes

Oman's foreign minister, Badr al-Busaidi, traveled to Tehran to meet his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, where the two described their talks as constructive and released a joint statement outlining what they called "a phased framework that could provide a practical and implementable basis for moving forward." The framework includes establishing a temporary joint navigational corridor through the strait and a joint project to clear mines from it, with al-Busaidi saying afterward that he hoped the two countries would "soon announce" the corridor and practical arrangements to restore safe navigation. A permanent solution and long-term governance of the strait, the statement said, would follow later.

Iran has insisted that inbound ships use a northern route through its own territorial waters, while the U.S. military has spent months protecting tankers using a separate southern route that hugs Oman's coastline. U.S. Central Command has said more than 660 million barrels of crude oil have exited the strait under its protection along that southern corridor since May, even as sporadic attacks on shipping in the region continued, including two cargo ships struck last week in an incident that killed two sailors.
Conflicting claims on the mines

The proposed mine-clearing mission was announced the same day President Trump said on social media that the U.S. Navy had already removed or detonated all mines from the strait's international waters, warning that Iran had been notified that any vessel caught laying new mines would be "immediately and systematically destroyed." Axios reported that U.S. officials corroborated the claim, saying the Navy had spent months using underwater drones to scan the strait's median shipping lane, identifying more than 100 suspected mines that private contractors were then hired to remove or destroy. Oman's reference to a still-pending mine-clearing mission appeared to sit uneasily alongside Trump's announcement, and it remains unclear how the two efforts relate.
Iran's weakening grip on the strait

The diplomatic overture comes as Iran's practical control over traffic through the strait has eroded sharply. Weekly vessel transits have surged from around 40 two weeks ago to nearly 200 more recently, with more than 80% of liquid cargo shipments either using the U.S.-backed Omani corridor or moving without transponders, likely along the same southern route Tehran has rejected. One oil-market analyst described the shift bluntly, saying it increasingly looks as though Iran has at least partially lost control of the strait. The strait became a flashpoint after war broke out earlier this year between Iran, the United States and Israel, and the current negotiations build on a June memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Iran aimed at ending that conflict. Qatar has voiced support for the talks, with its prime minister expected to travel to Tehran for follow-up discussions, and news of the proposed framework helped push oil prices lower for a third straight session as traders weighed the prospect of more Gulf crude reaching global markets.

articles.title: New UK prime minister abolishes science and technology department in Whitehall shake-up
articles.subtitle: Lawmakers warn the reorganization could fragment policy on artificial intelligence and research funding
articles.excerpt: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has dissolved the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, folding most of its responsibilities into a new business department while moving artificial intelligence policy directly into the Cabinet Office, a move that has unsettled parts of Britain's tech sector.
articles.author: elena-marsh

content.text: Britain's new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has abolished the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, dissolving the three-year-old ministry as part of a wider reorganization of Whitehall carried out shortly after he took office.
What changed

The department, created in 2023 by then-prime minister Rishi Sunak to bring science, technology and digital policy together under one roof, will see most of its functions absorbed into a newly formed Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, while responsibility for digital transformation and online harms moves instead to the Department for Culture, Media and Sport. The government has framed the change as a way to align technology policy more closely with economic strategy, arguing that folding research and innovation into the business department will produce a more coordinated national industrial strategy and reduce duplication across government.
Who moved where

Jonathan Reynolds, who previously led the old business department before serving as chief whip, has returned to lead the new combined department, which inherits the Sovereign AI investment unit, the Advanced Research and Invention Agency and UK Research and Innovation, bringing research funding and commercialization policy under one roof for the first time. Artificial intelligence policy has been elevated rather than folded in: Kanishka Narayan, appointed minister of state for artificial intelligence, will work jointly across the Cabinet Office and the new business department and will attend cabinet meetings, a first for the AI brief. The AI Security Institute is expected to remain closely tied to the Cabinet Office as part of that arrangement. Liz Kendall, the outgoing science secretary who helped establish the Sovereign AI Fund, stepped down before the reshuffle was formally announced, as did Lord Patrick Vallance, the science minister and former government chief scientific adviser.
Reaction from the tech sector

The decision has unsettled parts of Britain's technology and investment community. In an open letter published before the reshuffle was confirmed, the industry groups TechUK and the Startup Coalition warned that the old department gave the sector "a single government partner that understands it," and that folding it into a larger structure risked diluting attention to fast-moving areas like artificial intelligence and life sciences just as momentum was building. Supporters of the change counter that embedding science and technology policy directly inside the government's economic engine room, rather than keeping it siloed in a standalone department, will make it easier to translate research into commercial growth. Parliament's own science and technology committee has said it expects to hear directly from ministers in the coming weeks about how the transition will be managed and which parts of government will take the lead on ongoing initiatives, including the country's AI adoption plans.

articles.title: Typhoon Dolphin slams China's coast as region endures busy storm season
articles.subtitle: The storm was the most powerful to hit the country so far this year
articles.excerpt: Typhoon Dolphin made a double landfall in eastern China's Zhejiang province with winds near 94 miles per hour, prompting the evacuation of more than a million people and the cancellation of over 1,300 flights as the region endures its most active typhoon season in years.
articles.author: elena-marsh

toc.text: Part of an unusually active season

content.text: Typhoon Dolphin made a double landfall on China's eastern coast in Zhejiang province on the evening of August 9, arriving as the most powerful storm to hit the country this year and triggering the highest level of typhoon alert issued by China's National Meteorological Center.
Landfall and mass evacuations

The storm first came ashore near Yuhuan in Taizhou with maximum sustained winds of roughly 151 kilometers per hour, or about 94 miles per hour, equivalent to a Category 1 hurricane, before making a second landfall in nearby Yueqing about 70 minutes later. Authorities evacuated more than a million people across the region, including roughly 900,000 residents relocated in the city of Wenzhou alone, where more than 1,000 emergency shelters were opened, along with about 390,000 people evacuated in Taizhou and tens of thousands more in Shanghai and neighboring Fujian province.

Coastal cities including Wenzhou, Taizhou and Ningbo activated Level I emergency response, the highest tier in China's four-level system, with Wenzhou ordering a citywide suspension of classes, work, production and transportation. Air travel across the region was badly disrupted, with Shanghai's Pudong and Hongqiao airports canceling more than 1,300 flights and Hangzhou's airport canceling nearly 400 more. Ferry and cruise services across Zhejiang and Fujian were suspended, and authorities in Fujian relocated construction crews and vessels away from offshore project sites as a precaution.

Search and rescue crews searched for a nine-year-old boy swept into the sea during the storm in the city of Wenling, according to local media. Forecasters warned that parts of Zhejiang could see 200 to 400 millimeters, or up to nearly 16 inches, of rain as Dolphin moved inland, raising the risk of flooding and landslides in mountainous areas. The storm continued tracking westward into central China in the days that followed, prompting Beijing to raise its own rainfall warnings and prepare to activate its flood control response.
Part of an unusually active season

Dolphin was the thirteenth named typhoon of the year in the northwest Pacific and the second storm this season to trigger China's highest-level red alert, following Typhoon Noul in late July. Forecasters have described the season as unusually active across the basin, in contrast to a comparatively quiet Atlantic hurricane season, with China, Japan and the Philippines all struck by separate storms in rapid succession earlier in the summer. The storm arrived within days of a separate tropical system that brought heavy rain to Hawaii, illustrating the wide geographic reach of this year's active Pacific storm pattern.
